articles.title: Quote of the Day by Leo Tolstoy: “A man is like a fraction whose numerator is what he is and whose denominator is...”
articles.summary: Leo Tolstoy was not merely one of the greatest novelists the world has produced; he was also a man who spent his life wrestling with some of the most
articles.body: Leo Tolstoy was not merely one of the greatest novelists the world has produced; he was also a man who spent his life wrestling with some of the most difficult questions of human existenc, love, marriage, death, faith, morality, wealth, war, family and the search for meaning. His extraordinary achievement was to turn these questions into stories populated by characters who felt startlingly real. More than a century after his death, his novels continue to speak to readers because his central concern was not a particular time or society, but the human condition itself.Born on September 9, 1828, at Yasnaya Polyana, his family's estate in Russia, Tolstoy belonged to the Russian aristocracy. He lost both his parents at a young age and was raised largely by relatives. As a young man, he entered Kazan University but left without completing his degree. His early adulthood was turbulent. He gambled, accumulated debts, pursued romantic relationships and struggled to find a sense of purpose.His experiences in the army, however, began to transform him. Tolstoy served in the Caucasus and later in the Crimean War. What he witnessed during military service gave him material for his early literary works, including Childhood and The Sevastopol Sketches. These writings established him as a serious young writer and revealed a quality that would remain central to his work: an extraordinary ability to observe people closely.Tolstoy's great novels came later. War and Peace, published between 1865 and 1869, combined sweeping historical events with intensely personal stories. what ultimately moved society.Then came Anna Karenina, one of the greatest novels ever written. Published in the 1870s, it begins with a marriage and an affair but expands into a profound examination of love, family, social expectations, jealousy, loneliness and the search for a meaningful life.What makes Tolstoy's writing remarkable is its psychological depth. His characters are rarely simply good or bad. They contradict themselves, change their minds, behave selfishly and then generously, experience guilt, desire, fear and hope. They often do not fully understand themselves. Tolstoy understood that human beings are complicated precisely because they are capable of holding conflicting emotions at the same time.His writing style was equally distinctive. He could move effortlessly from enormous historical events to the smallest detail of a person's expression or gesture. A battlefield, a ballroom, a family dinner and a private moment of despair could all receive the same intense attention. He avoided making his characters feel like literary constructions; instead, they seem to think and breathe independently of the author.But Tolstoy's life changed dramatically after his literary triumphs. In middle age, he experienced a profound spiritual and moral crisis. He married Sophia Behrs in 1862, and they had a large family. Sophia played an enormous role in managing the household and supporting his literary career, including repeatedly copying his manuscripts.responsibilities.Tolstoy died in 1910, aged 82, after leaving his home in search of a simpler existence. His final years had become almost symbolic of the conflict that had defined his life: a world-famous aristocratic writer trying to escape the privileges and possessions that had once defined him.His impact is difficult to overstate. War and Peace and Anna Karenina remain foundational works of world literature, while his ideas about non-violence influenced political and social movements far beyond Russia. His greatest legacy, however, may be his insistence that literature should make us look honestly at ourselves.Tolstoy did not simply write about people. He examined why people behave as they do and asked whether they could become better.Quote of the Day“A man is like a fraction whose numerator is what he is and whose denominator is what he thinks he is.”Leo Tolstoy's metaphor of the fraction is deceptively simple. The numerator represents what a person actually is his abilities, character, actions, achievements and perhaps his real contribution to the world. The denominator represents what he thinks he is his self-image, ego, ambitions and opinion of his own importance. The brilliance of the metaphor lies in what happens mathematically: the larger the denominator becomes, the smaller the fraction becomes. Imagine someone who is genuinely talented but believes he is extraordinary. His actual abilities may be considerable, but his inflated opinion of himself makes the overall “fraction” smaller. Conversely, a person who has modest abilities but does not exaggerate his importance may possess a healthier relationship with himself.Tolstoy was pointing towards one of the oldest human problems: the gap between who we are and who we imagine ourselves to be.Modern life makes this gap particularly relevant. Social media encourages people to construct carefully edited versions of themselves. Professional success can become an identity. Wealth, appearance, popularity, education and status can all become measures through which people decide how important they are. The danger begins when perception becomes more important than reality.The quote is therefore not simply about humility. It is about self-awareness. There is another layer to Tolstoy's idea: our self-image can also distort our understanding of failure. If we believe we must always be successful, a setback can feel like an attack on our identity. But if we understand ourselves honestly strengths and weaknesses included failure becomes information rather than humiliation. In that sense, the quote offers a powerful lesson for everyday life: the healthiest relationship with oneself comes from reducing the distance between reality and self-perception.The answer requires honesty. We may discover that we are less extraordinary than we imagined. But we may also discover that we are stronger, kinder, more capable or more resilient than we had given ourselves credit for. That is perhaps the real wisdom behind the metaphor. Self-knowledge is not about thinking less of yourself; it is about seeing yourself accurately. And for Tolstoy, that honest vision of oneself was the beginning of a more meaningful life.Tolstoy's metaphor of the fraction is deceptively simple. articles.title: 'Remain alert, stay indoors': India issues advisory for citizens in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia on Thursday issued an advisory to Indian nationals after several explosions were heard in Riyadh, including
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia on Thursday issued an advisory to Indian nationals after several explosions were heard in Riyadh, including a large blast at King Khalid International Airport. It urged them to remain alert, stay indoors as necessary and follow instructions issued by local authorities.“In view of the current situation, all Indian nationals in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia are advised to remain alert and vigilant, stay indoors as necessary, and follow the instructions issued by local authorities through official channels,” the embassy said.It further added, "Indian nationals are strongly advised to refrain from circulating or reposting any videos or news related to the ongoing events. The Embassy of India, Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah and its outsourced services through VFS, are continuing to function normally and will issue updates and advisories as and when necessary."Flights suspended, U-turn Air India and Lufthansa Group airlines have suspended flights to and from Riyadh amid the escalating security situation in Saudi Arabia following attacks claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.Air India and Air India Express cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 10, according to the officials.Lufthansa Group airlines will suspend flights to Riyadh through October 16, a spokesperson for the German group said. The spokesperson cited “current developments in the Middle East” for the decision.Earlier, an Air India flight from Delhi to Riyadh was also turned around and is returning to Delhi after the attacks on Saudi airports raised concerns over the safety of airspace in the region. Flight AI2243 had departed from Delhi and was flying south over Gujarat before proceeding over the Arabian Sea. The pilots subsequently turned the aircraft around and began flying back towards Delhi.The U-turn came after Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia left one person dead and eight injured, according to the latest information. The developments also came as smoke was seen rising from a stationary aircraft at Riyadh airport.The flight suspensions came as King Khalid International Airport was temporarily disrupted following the explosions heard in Riyadh. The airport had earlier issued an advisory asking passengers to remain in contact with their respective airlines for information on flight status.Flightradar24 said on Thursday that King Khalid International Airport had “closed again.”Embassy issues helpline for IndiansThe embassy said its 24x7 Pravasi Bharatiya Sahayata Kendra helpline remains available at 8002471234 and advised the Indian community to follow the embassy's official social media handles for updates.It also strongly advised Indian nationals against circulating or reposting videos or news related to the ongoing events.“The Embassy of India, Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah and its outsourced services through VFS, are continuing to function normally and will issue updates and advisories as and when necessary,” it said.READ ALSO: Musk goes on rant after India rejects ‘oligarch’ claim: What makes Starlink controversialIndia condemns attacks on Saudi airportsIndia had on Wednesday condemned attacks targeting Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in recent days, which Saudi authorities said killed three people and injured several others.“India condemns the attacks that targeted Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh during the past few days, which resulted in the deaths and injuries of civilians. Targeting civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable,” the ministry of external affairs said.“We extend our sincerest condolences to the families of those who lost their loved ones, and we wish a speedy recovery to the injured. We also express our solidarity and stand with the people and government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” it added.Smoke seen at Riyadh airport as flights haltedSmoke was seen rising from a stationary aircraft at Riyadh airport on Thursday, according to a witness and three people briefed on the matter.Fire and ambulance crews were deployed at the airport and smoke was visible, the witness said. Outgoing flights were halted and passengers were instructed to leave their checked-in luggage behind and evacuate the airport.The cause of the explosions was not immediately known and there was no immediate independent confirmation of what caused the blast or how many flights were affected.Houthis claim missile strike on King Khalid airportThe Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed they had struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile.The Houthis have repeatedly claimed attacks against airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in recent days.Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Three killed in recent airport attacksThe latest explosions came a day after Saudi officials said attacks claimed by the Houthis on King Khalid airport and Abha airport had killed three people.The King Khalid attack killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight others, while the Abha attack killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and injured 28 people, officials said.The attacks have raised concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, as the kingdom becomes increasingly involved in the latest front of the Iran war.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Musk goes on rant after India rejects ‘oligarch’ claim: What makes Starlink controversial
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: SpaceX CEO and the world's richest man Elon Musk on Thursday went on a rant explaining how the Starlink's satellite internet services will help
articles.body: NEW DELHI: SpaceX CEO and the world's richest man Elon Musk on Thursday went on a rant explaining how the Starlink's satellite internet services will help the "least served" in India. Musk had just a day earlier alleged that his telecom firm was facing regulatory hurdles in India due to "oligarchs", a claim which was strongly rejected by the Indian government.Also read: Rahul Gandhi reacts to Musk's remarks; Starlink boss says 'thank you'The SpaceX chief then launched a tweet blitz posting about thrice in just a span of 10 minutes."Starlink will help the least-served in India," he said in a post at 6:18pm.He followed it up with another post at 6:25pm, writing, "Starlink provides Internet connectivity to the least-served, enabling self-education and prosperity by giving people access to sell their products worldwide!"Three minutes later, Elon posted again: "People who oppose @Starlink hurt only the least-served. The wealthy or those living in large cities already have good Internet, so they don’t understand."Musk's comments come as a Starlink delegation is attending the India Mobile Congress organised in the national captial.Musk's claim about Starlink serving the "least-served" in India is somewhat ironic, as India already ranks among the countries with the lowest internet charges in the world."The last decade was about scalability, penetration, affordability. We have discussed many times of how voice prices have crashed, data prices have lowered by almost 97%, which has led to greater penetration," information & technology minister Jyotiraditya Scindia said on Thursday.On the other hand, Starlink will reportedly cost Rs 8,600 per month, with an additional Rs 34,000 one-time hardware charge.What Musk claimed & what the govt replied"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are … This is a crime against the people of India!" Musk said in a post on Wednesday.The telecom ministry rejected Musk's claim stating, "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all three licensees""The Department of Telecom has issued licences to all satcom companies as well as provisional spectrum. Now the issue is pending with MHA for security clearance. As soon as it is cleared, they will get it. It has nothing to do with one company," minister of state for communications Chandra Sekhar Pemmasani told reporters on the sidelines of the India Mobile Congress.READ ALSO: 'Remain alert, stay indoors': India issues advisory for citizens in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacksWhy Starlink has sparked controversyThe logic behind Starlink is simple: Get internet to places where conventional networks are difficult or too expensive to reach. But Elon Musk’s satellite internet service has increasingly become much more than a tool for connectivity. Its growing use in war zones, conflict areas and during internet shutdowns has turned Starlink into a strategic technology and raised questions over who controls access to it.Critics have raised concerns about the company’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, arguing that a privately controlled satellite network could have implications for national security and sovereignty.How does Starlink workStarlink uses thousands of small satellites in low-Earth orbit, around 550km above the planet. Unlike traditional communications satellites positioned around 36,000km away, these satellites can transmit data with lower latency. Users connect through a small receiver with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically links with satellites passing overhead. The satellites can also transfer data between themselves using laser links.What are the major concernsA 2024 report by the Kutniti Foundation, had described Starlink as “a wolf in sheep’s clothing”. The foundation argued that Starlink’s global satellite network gives it capabilities that go beyond conventional telecom services and could create strategic concerns for countries such as India.US intelligence links: Kutniti has highlighted Starlink’s links with US intelligence and military agencies, including publicly known contracts involving Musk’s companies.Dual-use technology:The foundation argues that Starlink can provide high-speed internet while also supporting capabilities such as high-definition imagery and live video transmission.Control beyond borders: Unlike traditional telecom networks that rely on infrastructure within a country, Starlink’s satellites operate from outside national territory, raising questions over regulatory control.Security requirements: Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has said Starlink has not yet fulfilled all required security conditions. India’s licence will be issued only after those requirements are met.Furthermore, the satellites also raise security questions. Satellites travel at roughly 11,000 km/h to 28,000 km/h orbiting the earth and can also be used to monitor activity inside the territory of a country.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Alwar ‘detention’ takes a twist: CJP claims Deepak Baliyan assaulted, brother injured; Rajasthan Police deny action
articles.summary: ALWAR: The controversy over the alleged detention of Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) national organisation co-incharge Deepak Baliyan took a fresh turn on
articles.body: ALWAR: The controversy over the alleged detention of Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) national organisation co-incharge Deepak Baliyan took a fresh turn on Thursday after party leaders claimed that Rajasthan Police had detained him and assaulted him and his brother, even as police maintained that Baliyan had not been detained.Baliyan, a resident of Mankheda village in Alwar district, had earlier accused local police of placing him under house arrest and threatening his family ahead of the CJP’s October 10 protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The CJP had initially claimed that Baliyan was "forcibly picked up" from his home by Rajasthan Police. Party leader Ashutosh Ranka later called on party supporters to reach the Kathumar police station.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke subsequently alleged that the incident had escalated, claiming that Rajasthan Police had assaulted Baliyan and his brother.“Rajasthan Police has brutally assaulted CJP spokesperson Dipak Balyan and his brother followed by a stern warning by Ashutosh Ranka.... This is the twist.Deepak has been detained and his brother’s head has been cracked open,” Dipke posted on X.Responding to Dipke's post, part leader Ashotosh Ranka said: “All cockroaches should immediately reach Kathumar Police Station, Alwar." Tagging the Rajasthan Police, Ranka further wrote: "Sab yaad rakha jaayega.”These allegations, however, are at odds with the Rajasthan Police's account. Kathumar SHO Chandrashekhar Sharma said he was in Faridabad searching for an accused and was unaware of anything involving Baliyan.Alwar SP Sudhir Chaudhary also dismissed the allegations as baseless, asserting that Baliyan had not been detained. He said police personnel were merely patrolling the area because of the ongoing panchayat elections and that Baliyan had been livestreaming the police patrol on social media.Baliyan, meanwhile, told TOI that nearly a dozen policemen had surrounded his residence around 7pm. He said the police initially stood close to his house but moved around 200 metres away after he questioned their presence and recorded a video. He also claimed that the road leading to his residence had been cordoned off from both ends.Baliyan alleged that his family had been threatened with being picked up by police at night and being implicated in cases carrying harsh legal sections that could make bail difficult. He also expressed concern for the safety of his family members, who he said were primarily engaged in farming.The developments come ahead of the CJP’s planned October 10 protest at Jantar Mantar against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise.“We are ready to be detained or arrested, but protest will be held on Oct 10 at Jantar Mantar,” Dipke had said.He had also questioned the restrictions on protests in Delhi, asking, “If Mumbai, Bengaluru can have peaceful protest, why Amit Shah not allowing it in Delhi,” PTI reported.Earlier on Thursday, Dipke, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee and actor-activist Prakash Raj led a protest in Bengaluru against Kumar, demanding his immediate resignation over alleged irregularities in the SIR of electoral rolls.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Ben Affleck opens up about losing both parents this year and his mother’s final words: “God, I thought 84 years would seem longer”
articles.summary: Ben Affleck covered plenty of ground in his recent Variety interview, from the future of movie stars to Batman and his new film Animals.
articles.body: Ben Affleck covered plenty of ground in his recent Variety interview, from the future of movie stars to Batman and his new film Animals.The 54-year-old spoke quietly to Variety about the loss of both his parents this year and the lessons that came with his mother’s final months.In the conversation he described a quiet comfort that can arrive with the death of parents at his age. “One of the things you grapple with at my age when parents die is there’s a comfort and awareness in knowing this is how it’s supposed to go,” he said. “When I go, it will be hard for my children, but none of us want it any other way.” He recalled his mother’s words near the end: “God, I thought 84 years would seem longer.” His own reply was simple. “I bet, because I thought 54 would seem longer.”A reminder about limited timeThat exchange stayed with him. “That’s what we get,” Affleck said. “We get this much time, and it’s a reminder not to put anything off or fix it later. It’s more about how you show up every day with everybody else.” He added that he felt lucky his mother did not face a more painful decline earlier in life.An adult relationship that arrived in timeWhile asked if he had said what he needed to, Affleck answered quickly. “My gosh, yeah. She’s an amazing woman.” Going through her belongings showed him a full life that existed apart from him. “You see this woman lived an entire lifetime that had nothing to do with me,” he said. The two had reached a stage of honesty that once felt impossible. “We got to have this nice adult relationship; we were really honest, and I was able to have discussions with her that I didn’t even imagine I would be able to when I was younger.”Choosing how the final chapter lookedHis mother faced a cancer diagnosis with clear-eyed decisions. “She had this cancer diagnosis, and a great lesson was the proactive way she said, ‘I’m going to make a decision about how much treatment I want to do and how that’s going to impact my life.’ She made her choices.” She wanted to keep seeing friends and stayed committed to being a grandmother. She refused to move to Los Angeles, kept her own routines, and still boarded a plane for any of her five grandchildren.How the loss settles into ordinary daysAs revealed by Affleck, the experience has shaped the way he moves through his current life. He spoke of shared custody, school pickups, and quiet dinners when the kids agree to stay at the table. “I have nothing salacious or all that interesting in my life,” he said. “I work hard, and then I go home and pick up the kids from school… They have a great thing with their mom, for whom I’m also really, really grateful.”The reflections sat quietly beside talk of work and business. In an industry that often rewards performance, the most lasting notes Affleck shared that day came from simply paying attention at home.

articles.title: In 1994, Bill Clinton signed a desert-protection law that impacted nearly 9.2 million acres of California, creating Mojave National Preserve and expanding Joshua Tree and Death Valley
articles.summary: Explore the impact of the California Desert Protection Act of 1994, signed by Bill Clinton, which protected over 9 million acres of California desert landscapes, establishing Mojave National Preserve and expanding Joshua Tree and Death Valley National Parks.
articles.body: A significant portion of the eastern Mojave had been designated as a national scenic area since 1981, while Death Valley and Joshua Tree had been national monuments since 1933 and 1936, respectively. Large portions of the surrounding terrain were completely outside the National Park System, and those labels provided genuine but limited protection. According to the National Parks Conservation Association, a Barstow organisation called Citizens for Mojave National Park began advocating for something greater as early as 1976. Conservationists worked for decades to achieve this goal.That battle ultimately succeeded when President Bill Clinton signed the California Desert Protection Act on 31 October 1994. The Bureau of Land Management says the law impacts nearly 9.2 million acres of public land from the northern end of Death Valley to the Mexican border. It was sponsored by California’s two senators, Dianne Feinstein and Barbara Boxer.What the law foundThe act did three important things for the national parks. It changed Death Valley National Monument into Death Valley National Park and added over 1.3 million acres. It changed Joshua Tree National Monument into Joshua Tree National Park and added around 234,000 acres. And it established the Mojave National Preserve, some 1.4 million acres, in the previous East Mojave National Scenic Area.According to the Bureau of Land Management, the act established 74 additional wilderness areas in the California desert, totalling 7,661,069 acres across land maintained by the National Park Service, the Bureau of Land Management and the Forest Service. It also gave the state 20,500 acres of federal land to expand Red Rock Canyon State Park.Clinton's signing statement, available through the National Archives, stated that some 7.7 million acres had been declared as wilderness and another 3 million acres added to the National Park System. The Bureau of Land Management later tallied about 9.2 million acres as subject to the law, a figure that reflects the combined wilderness and park expansion rather than a separate count.Parks, preserves and wildernessThe Mojave National Preserve, though it is called a preserve and not a park, is managed under the National Park System laws of the act. The statute also created advisory commissions for Joshua Tree and Death Valley, which provided advice on management plans in the years that followed.Death Valley was changed most of all. The park now totals more than 3.3 million acres with the 1994 expansions, and the National Parks Conservation Association said it became the largest national park unit outside Alaska. Its size implies it can protect entire desert basins and mountain ranges, rather than just small sections. Private generosity filled in some of the gaps. According to the Bureau of Land Management, The Wildlands Conservancy donated more than 560,000 acres to join up scattered "checkerboard" parcels inside the Mojave Preserve and the surrounding wilderness areas.Why the law still mattersAs the bill moved through Congress, the Christian Science Monitor called it the largest public lands law since the Wilderness Act of 1964. Now Joshua Tree, Death Valley and Mojave are connected in a protected chain of desert land spanning Southern California, with wilderness areas around them cushioning wildlife habitat from traffic and development.The National Park Service has a summary of the act that explains the legal foundation for each park, including the findings Congress made concerning safeguarding the Mojave Desert. The practical outcome for visitors is the long-term protection of three quite distinct desert landscapes through national park designation. It was a major land-protection act in California history and continues to shape desert management.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2016, Barack Obama expanded that Hawaiian ocean refuge by 442,781 square miles, creating a protected area nearly the size of the Gulf of Mexico
articles.summary: In a landmark decision, President Obama expanded the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument by 442,781 square miles, establishing the largest protected area on Earth to safeguard marine biodiversity and cultural heritage.
articles.body: For almost a century, the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands, a group of small, isolated islands and atolls located far to the northwest of the main Hawaiian Islands, have been considered unique. According to the Department of the Interior, protection started with bird reservations and expanded into the Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge in 1940. The Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, which spans 139,797 square miles of water, was established by President George W. Bush in 2006. Scientists found that deep-water life extended beyond the monument's bounds, and the site was inscribed as a mixed natural and cultural UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.A proclamation signed by President Barack Obama on August 26, 2016, significantly changed the monument's scale. The monument’s own Papahānaumokuākea website report explains that the enlargement included 442,781 square miles, bringing the total protected area to 582,578 square miles, roughly the size of the Gulf of Mexico. That made Papahānaumokuākea one of the largest protected areas on Earth at the time.How the expansion happenedThe expansion proposal had a clear lead-up. In June 2016, Hawaii Senator Brian Schatz submitted it to President Obama, marking the tenth anniversary of the original monument. Early August saw public forums held on Oʻahu and Kauaʻi and on 25 August Governor David Ige wrote to the president confirming his support. The decision was also made in consultation with Native Hawaiian leaders, cultural organisations, conservation organisations, scientists and fishermen, the White House said.Science was a key factor. The White House said new exploration had revealed new species and deep-sea habitats and important ecological links between the existing monument and the waters beside it. The monument was expanded under the Antiquities Act, which lets presidents protect federal lands and waters by proclamation, and according to the monument's own figures, the move more than quadrupled the original protected area.What the new protections permitAccording to the White House fact sheet, no commercial resource extraction is permitted in the expanded area, including commercial fishing or future mineral mining. By permit, noncommercial fishing (including recreational fishing and fish removal for Native Hawaiian traditional customs) and scientific study are authorised.The fishing issue drew strong opposition. National Geographic said Hawaii's longline fleet strongly opposed the expansion, since boats that had fished in the newly protected waters would have to halt. The White House, in turn, cited Hawaii’s carefully managed longline fleet as a world leader in environmentally friendly techniques and said the decision built on a long legacy of marine conservation in Hawaiian waters.Why the waters matterThe White House said the extension provides crucial protection for more than 7,000 marine species, including whales and sea turtles listed under the Endangered Species Act. It also features black coral, a specimen of which NOAA has estimated to be more than 4,500 years old, among the longest-living marine species known. The extended region is a sacred site in Native Hawaiian culture and part of traditional voyaging and wayfinding, and it also holds historically significant wrecks of ships and planes from the Battle of Midway during World War II.NOAA scientists examined deep seas in and around the monument earlier in 2016 using a remotely operated vehicle, capturing deep marine life at depths ranging from around 2,130 feet to 2.7 miles. Some of that film was shot outside the bounds of the monument originally, as NOAA’s Earth is Blue feature outlines, and is now protected.Papahānaumokuākea is a good example for anyone attempting to understand why ocean protection became a big component of the discourse around conservation. It shows how a remote chain of islands, a decade of monument protection and fresh scientific findings have led to a vast region of open ocean being blocked to commercial extraction, while still allowing for cultural activities and research.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2024, Sydney laid a road using fibres from discarded coffee cups and a petroleum-free binder; 15,600 heavy vehicles crossed it in 75 days as tests indicated improved durability
articles.summary: Sydney has trialed a new road surface made from discarded coffee cups and a sustainable binder, demonstrating enhanced durability and reduced carbon emissions under heavy traffic conditions.
articles.body: A Sydney road trial has turned waste and renewable materials into a working asphalt surface. In February 2024, workers laid a section of temporary road at Sydney Water’s Upper South Creek Advanced Water Recycling Centre in Kemps Creek using cellulose fibres recovered from discarded coffee cups and a petroleum-free bio-binder.According to Sydney Water, the trial tested whether waste-derived and renewable materials could withstand demanding construction traffic. Over 75 days, more than 15,600 heavy-vehicle movements were recorded across the trial area. The utility later reported that the experimental asphalt appeared to show improved durability and allowed the pavement to be laid thinner than the conventional comparison surface. As road builders look for ways to reduce the environmental impact of conventional asphalt, the Sydney project tested whether waste fibres and renewable materials could perform on roads carrying heavy traffic.From discarded cups to road-building materialDisposable coffee cups are difficult to recycle. Although they are largely made from paper, many have a thin plastic lining that makes conventional recycling more complicated. Research suggests that this fibre-rich material can be recovered and used in asphalt mixtures. A study published in Construction and Building Materials examined shredded coffee cups as a substitute for conventional cellulose fibres used in stone mastic asphalt. The researchers found that small quantities could reduce binder drain-down while maintaining performance comparable to commercial cellulose fibre.The Sydney project used PAKPAVE, a cellulose-fibre product made from waste coffee cups collected through Closed Loop’s Simply Cups program. Sydney Water also notes that each tonne of trial asphalt contained the equivalent of 364 coffee cups. Should the process eventually become a part of the project for permanent internal roads, then the organisation had expected to save up to 415,000 cups from being sent to landfill. The asphalt was also manufactured using SAMIGreen, a polymer-modified, petroleum-free binder containing biogenic materials. This differed from conventional bitumen, which is typically derived from petrochemicals.A thinner road takes on heavy trafficThe trial used stone mastic asphalt containing recycled coffee-cup fibres and bio-binder, laid to a thickness of about 35mm over approximately 295 square metres. This was paired with a traditional pavement construction using around 45mm of asphalt. It was not just a question of economising on the use of materials. Sydney Water tests showed that the recycled fibre and bio-binder mix could produce a more durable pavement, allowing for a thinner layer. Both the trial pavement and the control pavement used 25 tonnes of material.The traffic provided the strongest real-world test. More than 15,600 heavy-vehicle movements took place on the pavement during the 75-day trial. The project initially reported the figure as more than 14,600 movements, which was later revised to more than 15,600. The project reported a 25% reduction in carbon emissions compared with SMA and a 14% reduction compared with dense-graded asphalt. The difference reflected the project's assessment of the materials, pavement thickness and the baseline used for each comparison.What the Sydney experiment could mean for future roadsThe process is attractive because it addresses two problems at once. Hard-to-recycle coffee cups can be used as a fibre, while a part of the oil-based binder can be substituted with a sustainable material. In Sydney, the experiment concerned a temporary road only and is not evidence that all roads can instantly be constructed with the help of coffee-cup fibres and bio-binder. The project says it has not yet been decided whether the mix will be used on permanent roads at the facility.Nevertheless, the test provided something a laboratory could not: real-world traffic from thousands of heavy vehicles. The test showed that pavement made from recycled coffee cups could be manufactured, laid, and tested under heavy construction traffic alongside an asphalt control section. If the materials continue to meet engineering standards, coffee cups may find a new use in Sydney roads.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Bypolls results 2026: Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Assam and Puducherry brace for closely watched verdicts
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Votes cast in five assembly constituencies and one Lok Sabha seat will be counted on Friday, with the results of the bypoll elections likely to
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Votes cast in five assembly constituencies and one Lok Sabha seat will be counted on Friday, with the results of the bypoll elections likely to be closely watched for broader political signals.The elections were held on October 6 in five assembly seats — Nandigram and Rejinagar in West Bengal, Madurantakam and Dharapuram in Tamil Nadu and Thattanchavady in Puducherry. The Lok Sabha seat of Nagaon in Assam also went to polls. Counting of votes will begin at 8am.The contests are not necessarily referendums on the governments in power, but they have acquired significance because they come at different points in the political transitions taking place in these states, particulary Tamil Nadu and West Bengal.BJP's first poll after the mega Bengal victoryThe spotlight will be firmly on West Bengal, where the BJP replaced the TMC after 15 years in power. The Nandigram and Rejinagar results would perhaps offer an early indication of how the BJP is performing after moving from the opposition to government.Turnout was high in both seats, with nearly 80 per cent of the 5.24 lakh electors voting. Nandigram recorded 80.89 per cent polling and Rejinagar 80.08 per cent.The polling, however, was not without controversy as there were allegations of voter intimidation, booth-level irregularities and sporadic clashes. The arrest of Aam Janata Unnayan Party chief Humayun Kabir after a confrontation with police in Rejinagar and Congress' demand for repolling in both seats added to the political tension.Nandigram carries particular weight because of its history as the constituency was central to the anti-land acquisition movement that helped bring the TMC to power in 2011. Suvendu Adhikari defeated Mamata Banerjee there in the 2021 Assembly election and won the seat again in 2026, while retaining Bhabanipur, leading to the bypoll.The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, whose son Chandranath Rath, a former aide of Adhikari, was shot dead two days after the BJP won the Assembly election. Her candidature therefore added an emotional element to the contest.The Opposition vote is also divided as the TMC faction led by Mamata Banerjee withdrew its candidate and backed Congress nominee Milan Pradhan. A rival TMC faction led by Ritabrata Banerjee is contesting separately. The result could therefore indicate whether opposition coordination can translate into votes or whether the division benefits the BJP.Rejinagar presents a different contest where Humayun Kabir, who had won both Rejinagar and Nowda in the Assembly election, retained Nowda, leaving Rejinagar vacant. His AJUP has fielded his son Golam Nabi Azad. The contest includes candidates from the BJP, Mamata-led TMC, rival TMC faction, Congress and CPI(M).With a sizeable minority electorate, Rejinagar is particularly important for parties trying to consolidate or expand their respective support bases. For the Mamata-led TMC faction, it is also a test of whether it can retain support without relying on the familiar party name and symbol.Tamil Nadu tests TVK's early popularityTamil Nadu's Madurantakam and Dharapuram bypolls will also be closely watched, particularly because they are the first electoral test for the TVK government after it came to power in May.The AIADMK is seeking to win back the two seats it lost to the TVK in the April Assembly election, making the results an early measure of whether the new ruling party has retained its electoral momentum.Madurantakam recorded 86.26 per cent turnout, while Dharapuram saw 80.30 per cent polling. Both figures were lower than in the Assembly election five months ago. Turnout fell by nearly seven percentage points in Madurantakam and about 9.5 percentage points in Dharapuram.Counting centres in both constituencies have been placed under three-tier security. The EVMs and VVPAT units were moved to sealed strongrooms after polling, with round-the-clock surveillance and central and state security personnel deployed at the sites.Assam and Puducherry complete the day's pictureIn Assam, the Nagaon Lok Sabha bypoll is being seen as a three-way contest between BJP candidate and former bureaucrat Devasish Sharma, Congress nominee and former MLA Sibamoni Bora, and AIUDF chief Mohammed Badruddin Ajmal.The seat fell vacant after Congress MP Pradyut Bordoloi, who had won Nagaon for a second consecutive term in 2024, left the party, contested the Dispur Assembly seat on a BJP ticket and won it.Around 76 per cent of Nagaon's 19.05 lakh electors voted. Fifteen candidates are in the fray, although the contest is expected to be primarily between the BJP, Congress and AIUDF candidates.In Puducherry, the Thattanchavady Assembly bypoll recorded 80.8 per cent turnout. The seat fell vacant after AINRC chief and Chief Minister N Rangasamy resigned from it while retaining Mangalam.By the end of Friday, the results across these six contests would provide more than individual winners and losers. In West Bengal, they will offer an early look at the BJP's ability to consolidate power and at the opposition's ability to regroup. Tamil Nadu will provide an initial test of the TVK's popularity after its assembly victory, while Nagaon will show how the BJP, Congress and AIUDF fare in a three-way contest.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: US charges former Venezuela president Maduro with conspiracy to torture opponents
articles.summary: US authorities have added torture allegations to the criminal case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, accusing him of helping oversee a
articles.body: US authorities have added torture allegations to the criminal case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, accusing him of helping oversee a system of abuse aimed at silencing political opponents and keeping his government in power.The revised indictment, unsealed on Thursday, charges Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, with conspiring to commit torture. Maduro was already facing US charges over an alleged conspiracy to send cocaine into the country.The new allegations accuse Maduro of authorising torture, arbitrary detention and violence against opponents during his time as president. The indictment says thousands of Venezuelans were “harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed” by people acting at the direction of his government.It alleges that methods of abuse included electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation. In one case, Maduro allegedly threatened to have a prisoner's child killed “as a form of psychological torture.”Three US citizens among alleged victimsThe indictment details alleged involvement by Venezuela's military intelligence agency, DGCIM, which for years was headed by Gen. Hugo Carvajal, one of Maduro's co-defendants.Carvajal later broke with Maduro, pleaded guilty in New York last year to drug trafficking charges and has offered to testify against his former leader.The revised indictment says three US citizens were among those allegedly tortured, although their identities were not disclosed.One was allegedly punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months in detention. Another was allegedly beaten so severely that he needed a lengthy hospital stay and had a gun placed in his mouth.The third was allegedly handcuffed, hooded and beaten every half hour for two days, resulting in permanent damage to an eye.Maduro has previously faced lawsuits in US courts brought by Americans who said they were beaten while detained in Venezuela. He has denied wrongdoing.Maduro has also been under investigation by the International Criminal Court for years over alleged crimes against humanity linked to his crackdown on political opponents.Flores seeks house arrest on health groundsFlores appeared in court on Thursday as her lawyers asked for her release from jail and sought permission for her to remain under house arrest because of health problems.Her lawyers argued that she has medical conditions that cannot be properly treated in prison and could instead be kept at a New York residence under 24-hour security. They said she had suffered permanent scarring after being “thrown against a wall or dresser” during the US operation that led to her capture.Flores, 69, has lost 25 pounds, or about 11 kg, while being held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, according to her lawyers. They said doctors had told her she might require heart surgery and that she continues to suffer from “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath”. They also said she may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.Prosecutors opposed her release, describing her as an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public”. They said she had already been taken to a local hospital when medical treatment was required.Both Maduro and Flores have been in custody in New York since early January, when US forces seized them from their home in Caracas in a night-time operation.Both deny US drug chargesMaduro and Flores have pleaded not guilty to the cocaine trafficking case, which was first brought years ago against them and several alleged co-conspirators. A conviction could have resulted in life imprisonment.Their lawyers have also asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing that Maduro and Flores are protected by immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.The Trump administration has described the operation that captured Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation”. Maduro has described himself as a prisoner of war and called his capture a kidnapping.Flores is accused of joining her husband in the alleged cocaine importation conspiracy. Her lawyers have argued that she does not pose a flight risk because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Millions are watching Ash Dykes travel through the Congo Basin. Why do we love watching other people put themselves through extreme adventures?
articles.summary: From morbid curiosity to emotional investment, psychologists explain why we become hooked on watching strangers take extraordinary risks.
articles.body:
Millions of people are following extreme adventurer Ash Dykes on social media as he attempts to kayak 434 miles through the Congo Basin, which is considered one of the most hazardous and remote environments in the world.

Starting this week, the 35-year-old will travel in an inflatable kayak through waters inhabited by crocodiles and hippos, potentially encountering gorillas and elephants along the way. Consisting of 500 million acres of land and the second-largest river basin in the world, the Congo Basin is a hotspot for tropical diseases and is classed as unsafe to travel due to health, crime, unrest, terrorism and kidnapping risks, according to the State Department .

In a social media post outlining the challenge , Dykes warned he could be "days away from proper medical help" at some of the most remote points of the journey.

With more than 4.5 million followers across social media, Dykes has built a reputation for undertaking increasingly extreme adventures, including becoming the first person to trek across Mongolia solo and unsupported, and the first person on record to walk the entire length of the Yangtze River in China. His adventures have attracted huge audiences, including followers genuinely concerned for his welfare.

Dykes is documenting his Congo Basin journey online as it unfolds, turning an extreme expedition into episodic social entertainment with no guaranteed outcome.

While some social media users seem to be watching the footage through their fingers, others appear torn between excitement and anxiety.

"I hate that we all have to do this," one TikTok user commented on the adventurer's arrival video. "I'm stuck between wanting to experience this and blocking you because I don't want stress," another added.

As audiences follow these extraordinary missions in real time, why do we become so invested in watching a stranger take on a potentially dangerous challenge — and why does finding out whether they make it begin to feel so personal?

For those watching Dykes navigate the Congo Basin from the comfort of their homes, the appeal of such a dangerous expedition may go beyond simple entertainment.

Our fascination with watching others face danger is rooted partly in what psychologists call "morbid curiosity," an interest in threatening or potentially dangerous situations that allows us to learn about risks without experiencing them ourselves.

"There is no better way to safely learn about something dangerous than to witness it," Coltan Scrivner, an author and psychologist at Arizona State University, told Yahoo. "Our mind treats these opportunities for high-consequence learning as particularly valuable, which draws us to stories of danger."

But curiosity is only part of the appeal. Pamela Rutledge, director of the Media Psychology Research Center in Boston, said watching someone voluntarily undertake an extreme challenge also offers the excitement of danger without the physical consequences.

"Watching from a safe distance lets us experience the excitement of danger without facing the consequences ourselves," she said.

For some viewers, particularly those drawn to sensation-seeking, that can make following a risky adventure especially rewarding. Yet it doesn't entirely explain why audiences continue watching when the experience makes them anxious.

Mary Beth Oliver, a professor of media studies at Penn State University, points to a media theory known as "excitation transfer," which suggests that the heightened arousal created by suspense can intensify our emotional response to what happens next.

"Ultimately, I don't think people want to experience anxiety, but that anxiety can heighten our feelings of elation when the character wins or avoids danger," she said.

Oliver compared it to watching a close sporting match. While a win usually feels good, a last-minute victory can feel far more satisfying than an easy victory because of the way the tension builds until the final moment.

Dykes' followers will be left in suspense as they await the next update. As the expedition unfolds, each new social media post offers a snapshot of his progress while leaving the outcome of the wider journey unresolved.

"Each post is a mini-cliffhanger that encourages continued engagement," Rutledge said.

The serialized format is not unique to Dykes and has a long history in entertainment. Victorian novelists published their stories in installments, keeping readers coming back for the next chapter while creating a lucrative publishing model.

More recently, adventure creators such as British YouTuber Ed Pratt, who documented his journey around the world on a unicycle , and British YouTuber GeoWizard, known for attempting to cross countries in a straight line , have built audiences around ambitious, self-imposed challenges.

For Rutledge, the episodic nature of these adventures is part of their appeal.

"Each post is one installment of the journey and becomes a piece of a puzzle leading to the next post," she said.

While the creators' missions differ, each has a clearly defined goal and obstacles to overcome. Dykes has taken this a step further by releasing social media clips documenting his adventure in real time.

When spectators become emotionally invested

As viewers become familiar with Dykes' personality, decisions and setbacks through repeated updates, their curiosity about the adventure can develop into genuine concern for his welfare.

"The question moves from being outcome-oriented: Can this guy kayak 434 miles through the Congo Basin? to a more relational perspective as we get to know Dykes as a person and become more sensitive to the risks he faces," Rutledge said.

This can be explained in part by parasocial relationships , the one-sided connections audiences develop with people they repeatedly encounter through the media.

"The uncertainty and danger threaten someone the viewers feel they know," she said.

But that emotional investment is not necessarily unhealthy.

"Parasocial relationships are, for the most part, beneficial; they can create feelings of belonging and decrease loneliness," the academic said.

While the relationship with Dykes may be one-sided, sharing his journey on social media allows those interested in the adventure to connect and share their anticipation.

"The journey becomes both a vicarious experience and a shared social event," Rutledge said.

For the millions following Dykes' journey, the adventure is far from over. Until the next update arrives, they'll have to keep waiting to find out.

articles.title: In 2016, Washington installed 26 human-made beaver dams in a damaged creek; after one flood, sediment rose nearly 5 feet, and water depth increased 11%
articles.summary: Discover how Washington state restored Myers Creek with human-made beaver dams, improving sediment retention, water depth, and encouraging beaver populations to return.
articles.body: In eastern Washington, a damaged creek received an unusual form of help in 2016. Instead of rebuilding the channel with conventional engineering structures, restoration workers installed 26 human-made structures designed to behave like beaver dams. Within months, the experiment was reshaping the stream, slowing water and allowing sediment to accumulate where erosion had previously deepened the channel.According to the Washington State Department of Ecology, the structures were installed along about 1,900 feet of Myers Creek as part of the Triple Creek restoration project. The creek had been badly altered by a major rain-on-snow event in the 1990s, which sent unusually large flows through the channel, deepened it and left steep banks while draining parts of the surrounding wetlands. When the beaver ponds that had once helped hold the floodplain in place disappeared, the drier ground also became more favourable to invasive plants. The restoration team therefore turned to what are known as Beaver Dam Analogues, or BDAs. They were intended to recreate some of the physical effects of natural beaver dams and, importantly, encourage beavers to return and eventually maintain the system themselves.Building a dam without the beaversThe structures at Myers Creek were simple. Wooden stakes measuring 3 to 6 inches in diameter were driven into the streambed, and branches were woven between them. Some structures were built across the streambed to slow the flow and retain sediment. Other structures served as deflection structures where the flow would be diverted towards the sides of the streambed, encouraging the channel to meander. The goal is not simply to create a series of ponds. Sediments could be retained through reducing the power of flowing water in the stream. The channel rose and reconnected with its natural floodplain.The Washington Department of Ecology also notes that the restoration team planted native vegetation and tackled reed canarygrass, an invasive plant that had become widespread after the creek became drier. The project included 14 planting sites and protection for other plants to help regenerate a riparian plant community that could restore shade, stability and food sources for returning beavers. However, there is one crucial difference between a natural beaver dam and a BDA. Unlike a natural beaver dam, a BDA cannot repair itself.According to research published in River Research and Applications, both natural beaver dams and beaver dam analogues can alter stream-channel conditions by slowing water, retaining sediment and influencing channel shape. The study found that these structures could promote sediment accumulation and modify local channel geomorphology, although their performance could vary during high-flow events. At Myers Creek, the 26 structures also interacted with the spring 2017 floodwaters, helping redirect flows, widen the incised channel and encourage sediment deposition instead of allowing the water to keep cutting through the channel.The results were significant. Sediment from the streambanks and upstream area built up by as much as 5 feet in some places, raising the streambed close to the historical floodplain. An annual survey in the first year after the high-flow events also found that water levels were more than 11% higher. The experiment thus revealed an important characteristic of such a restoration technique. The dams did not need to stay as solid structures to achieve the desired effect. Their interaction with water, sediment, and streambanks caused changes in the creek’s morphology.The beavers eventually returnedPerhaps the most notable result was what happened next, without any further action from the crew. Beavers came back to the area just days after construction started in 2016, despite their absence from the area for almost twenty years. At first, this created an unforeseen challenge because the beavers ate willow branches used in the habitat, so the crew switched to conifers and red-osier dogwood.By 2017, the beavers were doing more than just colonising the restored section. These beavers had constructed a dam at a site where weaving was not completed and had also contributed to the construction of another BDA. The beavers had even constructed a pioneer dam below the last structure installed. This was close to the project’s goal: using man-made structures to restore a degraded stream and encourage beavers and plant life to return.Triple Creek does not prove that man-made dams can fix every impaired water system. Their efficiency is determined by the state of the stream channel, availability of sediment material, plant cover, and water regime, as well as their maintenance. But Triple Creek suggests that, in a creek that has become too deep, fast and disconnected from its floodplain, mimicking beaver activity can help.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Palestine factions consider postponing elections amid Israeli complications, internal feud
articles.summary: Factions in Palestine consider postponing legislative elections in the country, which were supposed to happen after 20 years.
articles.body: Factions in Palestine consider postponing legislative elections in the country, which were supposed to happen after 20 years.President Mahmoud Abbas has set November 28 as the date of parliamentary elections in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.A top official with the Hamas-allied Islamic Jihad group told the Associated Press that the factions had reached an agreement to delay the vote.The reason for the postponement has been attributed to the logistical issues arising in Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem and war-struck Gaza, as well as the historical internal conflicts among the Palestinians.A spokesperson for President Abbas’ party Fatah, said the election timing will be part of a “dialogue and national consensus” among the factions. He did not clarify whether a final decision had been reached.The spokesperson also said that potential postponement will be discussed by the executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation.The Palestinian territories last held legislative elections in 2006, when Hamas defeated Abbas's Fatah party, which had previously dominated Palestinian politics. Since then, the Palestinian Legislative Council, the parliament of Abbas's Palestinian Authority, has not met since 2007.However, Palestinians did return to the polls in April, when they elected municipal council heads in the West Bank. That was the first vote since the Gaza war broke out in October 2023.On Tuesday, the European Union said it was ready to deploy election observers for the Palestinian legislative elections.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas made the announcement on X after speaking with Palestinian vice president Hussein Al-Sheikh."Palestinians have the right to choose their representatives in elections that are credible, inclusive and transparent," she wrote.Holding elections is among the reforms demanded by the international community, including the European Union.

articles.title: In 2013, Delaware spread carbon pellets across a polluted lake bottom in a US-first cleanup; the toxic chemicals were trapped and a new wetland improved habitat
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking cleanup effort, Delaware utilized activated carbon pellets to treat contaminated sediment in Mirror Lake, achieving significant reductions in toxic pollutants and enhancing local wildlife habitats.
articles.body: Nearly 80 tons of activated-carbon pellets were spread across the bottom of Mirror Lake in Dover, Delaware, in 2013, and state officials described it as the first full-scale application of the technology in the nation. The pellets were designed in such a way that they bind pollutants in contaminated sediment, which reduced the amount that was available to fish and other organisms.The project targeted a five-acre section of the upper St. Jones River watershed, since for decades, sediment at Mirror Lake had contained contaminants such as polychlorinated biphenyls, or PCBs, mercury and other pollutants. DNREC said those contaminants had contributed to concerns about fish consumption.The carbon stayed in the sedimentThe cleanup used a product called SediMite, which is a pelletized material that contains activated carbon. They were designed to sink through the water and break apart after reaching the sediment, and small organisms that lived in the lake bottom then helped incorporate the carbon into the biologically active sediment layer. Activated carbon works by adsorbing certain organic contaminants onto its surface, and at Mirror Lake, the treatment was carried out with the intention of increasing the sediment's ability so that they could hold pollutants such as PCBs.A 2020 paper in the Journal of Environmental Engineering described the project as the first full-scale remediation project in North America that directly placed activated carbon into lake sediments. The treatment covered a two-hectare lake and involved about 36 metric tons of activated carbon during a two-week application in November 2013.Monitoring found lower PCB exposureResearchers monitored sediment, porewater, surface water and fish after the treatment, and found reductions of 60% to 80% in freely dissolved PCBs in sediment porewater and surface water. Resident fish that were sampled three to five years after treatment had approximately 70% lower lipid-normalized PCB concentrations than before the cleanup. The monitoring period also gave researchers several years of data to assess whether the carbon treatment continued to affect contaminant exposure after the initial application.The researchers did not find the same change in every fish species, since two migratory species showed very limited reductions in PCB concentrations, which was attributed to their exposure outside Mirror Lake as they moved through the wider river system. The treatment was aimed at the contaminated sediment within the lake, not every potential source of PCBs in the watershed, which is why it is important to understand that distinction when assessing the results.A wetland was added beside the cleanupThe sediment treatment was combined with habitat restoration, where DNREC converted a sandbar into an intertidal wetland, added native plants and trees, and used coir logs to stabilize parts of the shoreline. The restoration gave the project a second objective that went beyond contaminant control, and DNREC said that the wetland increased the ecological function of the lake and helped improve conditions for fish and other wildlife. The agency also said that the combined cleanup and restoration made fish safer for people to eat.Monitoring data showed an approximately 80% reduction in PCB concentrations in sediment porewater and an approximately 70% reduction in resident fish by 2018, according to a summary published by Delaware officials of the peer-reviewed study. Mirror Lake became a field test for treating contaminated sediment without having to rely solely on conventional dredging, and DNREC later used an enhanced version of the approach at other contaminated sites in Delaware.You use AI every day. articles.body: British counter-terrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested near RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, a military base that houses US and Nato intelligence operations, police said Thursday.The men, aged 32 and 36, were found inside the base after Ministry of Defence Police discovered an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol and spotted a small breach in the perimeter fence. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Thursday challenged Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath to contest the upcoming assembly elections from Ayodhya. Akhilesh also said he would soon visit the Ram temple in Ayodhya along with SP leaders for darshan.Addressing a gathering at a Shrimad Bhagwat Katha organised by SP leader and former Ayodhya MLA Tej Narayan Pandey, also known as Pawan Pandey, Akhilesh claimed the BJP had conducted several surveys since the SP announced its candidate for the Ayodhya seat, reported news agency PTI."Ever since we announced our candidate, the BJP has been conducting survey after survey, and it is falling behind in every survey. We are hearing that they have not been able to find a new candidate for Ayodhya," Akhilesh said."If the chief minister, who makes tall claims, is so confident, he should contest the election from Ayodhya himself and prove it," he said.Later, responding to questions from reporters about visiting the Ram temple, Akhilesh said he had earlier decided to do so after the completion of the Kedareshwar Dham temple in Etawah."I had earlier resolved that after the completion of the Kedareshwar Dham, I would ask my party colleague Pawan Pandey to fix a date and we would all visit the Ram temple for darshan," he said.The clarification comes amid BJP's constant attack over his no visit to the Ram temple. articles.title: J-1 visa fraud: Harvard, Yale among 9 elite universities under investigation for alleged scam; 'Nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building'
articles.summary: Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT are under investigation for alleged visa fraud,
articles.body: Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Brown, the University of Pittsburgh, UC Davis, Caltech, Arizona State, and MIT are under investigation for alleged visa fraud, Vice President JD Vance announced, suggesting that these universities are exploiting the J-1 visa program to import cheaper students from overseas as an exchange program but only to evade higher payment to Americans. Unlike F-1 visa which is entirely student's visa, J-1 visa is meant for exchange students. It allows foreign nationals to work, study, train or teach in the US as part of a cultural and educational exchange. “Something weird is going on at these universities,” said Vance. “They’re using these visas way too much. They’re using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," Vance said.“Nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” said Labor Department watchdog Anthony D’Esposito, who reported that 61% of post-grad students at US universities come from overseas.“American taxpayers send billions of dollars to these universities to support research and innovation. They deserve to know where that money … is going, and whether it’s being used lawfully.”Not India but China is the targetUnlike H-1B, which always has its target on India, J-1 is allegedly being misused by China. D’Esposito said there are concerns that countries like China are taking advantage of the visa program to spy on American research and innovation. “The Chinese Communist Party doesn’t need to kick down the doors of America’s research laboratories if our own institutions are willing to leave the doors wide open,” he said.“If an American university is breaking the law to save $1 while exposing American research to a foreign adversary, that is not academic excellence. It’s institutional betrayal,” D’Esposito said.'Money won't protect you, neither will political connections'D'Esposito said the investigation against the nine elite universities is historic; subpoenas have been served. About 61% of postdoctoral researchers and federally funded workers at these institutions are foreign nationals. American taxpayers send billions of dollars to these universities to support research and innovation. They deserve to know where this money is going and whether it's being used lawfully."I spent my career as an NYPD detective. I worked on the streets of Brooklyn investigating violent criminals. who thought they were untouchable. I did not back down then and I sure as hell will not back down now. I don't care how prestigious a university thinks it is-- break the law and screw the American people and I will personally cuff you. I don't care how large your endowment is, how powerful you alumni are or how many politicians you have on speed dial," D'Esposito said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Palm Valley School closes after 74 years amid bankruptcy, leaving parents devastated; its 36-acre California campus with 53 classrooms is up for sale for $14 million
articles.summary: A 74-year-old private school in Southern California has been put up for sale for $14 million, just months after abruptly shutting its doors and filing for
articles.body: A 74-year-old private school in Southern California has been put up for sale for $14 million, just months after abruptly shutting its doors and filing for bankruptcy.The former campus of Palm Valley School (PVS) in Rancho Mirage is now on the market following the school’s closure in June, according to California Post. The sprawling 36-acre property includes separate buildings for its preschool, lower school, middle school and upper school, along with extensive sports and recreational facilities.According to the property listing, the campus features 53 classrooms, a full gymnasium, a science laboratory and an outdoor amphitheater. Its sports facilities include a baseball field, softball field, soccer/lacrosse/football field and basketball courts, as well as multiple parking areas.School closed after 74 yearsPalm Valley School was founded in 1952 and had operated from its Rancho Mirage campus since 1992. According to its website, which remains online despite the closure, it was the only private, co-educational, non-religious college-preparatory day school in the Coachella Valley.The school’s sudden closure came after months of uncertainty over its finances, leaving families and staff struggling to understand how an institution that had appeared to be preparing for another academic year could shut down so quickly.The school’s financial troubles first became known to parents in April, when administrators reportedly told families that PVS was exploring a potential partnership or merger with an international educational organisation, according to the Coachella Valley Independent.Parents were subsequently urged to submit enrollment contracts and deposits by May 1.Parents were told the school could stay openIn May, the school announced that it had received a financial gift that would allow it to remain open for the following academic year and potentially beyond.However, the optimism was short-lived.Just a week later, the school informed families that it was budgeting for 245 students for the 2026-27 academic year and would need to increase enrollment to address its ongoing financial challenges.By June, the situation had changed dramatically. Palm Valley School announced that it would file for Chapter 7 bankruptcy and would not reopen for the 2026-27 academic year.The abrupt decision left parents and employees feeling that they had been given false reassurance about the institution's financial position.Teacher says community was ‘devastated’Speaking to the Coachella Valley Independent, PVS teacher and parent Shaymi Ristaino said the school community had not been adequately informed about the severity of its financial problems.“The board didn’t approach us to find other ways to keep the school open. They had lied to us about where we were (financially) and about the families and teachers who were trying to raise money to help the school. It was devastating for me. I enjoyed working there,” Ristaino said.Ristaino not only lost her job following the closure but also said she did not receive back the enrollment fee she had paid for her daughter.You use AI every day.
