articles.title: In 2016, Michigan paved a school-bus route with recycled tyre rubber; after 3 years, inspectors found no visible cracking or rutting
articles.summary: In 2016, Michigan tested an innovative approach to road construction by using recycled tyre rubber in asphalt, resulting in no visible damage after three years. Discover how this eco-friendly initiative could change the future of pavement materials.
articles.body: Every school day, buses travelled along a residential road in Davison, Michigan, carrying children to and from school. In 2016, the road became the site of a less conventional experiment: part of its asphalt was made with rubber recovered from discarded tyres. According to the Transportation Research Board, the test was small, but its setting made it useful. The road, Cambridge Drive between S. State and S. Dayton Street, carried the city's school buses twice a day during the school year.It also provided access to an apartment complex and received direct sunlight, exposing the pavement to both regular traffic and Michigan's changing weather. Three years later, researchers inspecting the experimental section found little to complain about. The pavement showed no visible cracking or rutting, while its condition rating remained high. The result offered a practical glimpse into how waste tyres could be given a second life beneath everyday traffic.A road built with old tyresThe material used in Davison was not simply pieces of tyre scattered through the concrete. In the experiment conducted by the researchers, they used pre-conditioned dry-process ground tyre rubber, or DP-GTR. The rubber particles measured between 400 and 600 micrometres in diameter. The study also notes that the Michigan section used a nominal maximum aggregate size of 12.5 mm, 4.9% binder and 10% DP-GTR. Unlike the wet process, where rubber is blended into the bitumen before the asphalt mixture is produced, the dry process introduces the rubber directly into the mixture during production. The rubber becomes part of the aggregate-binder system as the asphalt is mixed, allowing the process to be carried out with only minor changes to conventional asphalt plant equipment.What happened after three years?Davison Road was a useful practical test because the mixture had to withstand vehicle traffic rather than laboratory conditions. Researchers examining the road in 2019 found no cracking or rutting in their visual observations. Using the PASER pavement rating method, the Michigan section scored 8.1. The laboratory results were less straightforward. The authors used different laboratory methods to test cracking and rutting resistance in the rubber-modified mixes. Some laboratory cracking tests were less favourable after rubber was added.The field observations helped contextualise those laboratory results. The researchers reported good-to-excellent performance across the field sections in Michigan, Illinois and Georgia, with limited cracking, rutting, and other visible distress. A separate study of crumb-rubber mixtures published in the International Journal of Pavement Research and Technology also found that field sections built in Michigan showed no rutting after five years of service, while some cracking appeared in neighbouring control lanes using conventional bitumen.Why the experiment matteredOld tyres are difficult waste because they are bulky, durable, and hard to dispose of traditionally. Using them as road material helps keep rubber in circulation while reducing the need for some virgin materials. The Michigan study also showed why pilot studies matter: asphalt blends can perform differently in real traffic than in the lab. The 2016 Davison project did not prove that all rubber-modified roads are more durable, and three years was not long enough to assess a pavement's full lifecycle. It was, however, a relatively small pavement test on a low-volume residential road. Still, the lack of cracking or rutting after three years was a positive result.The researchers' 2021 study concluded that pre-treated rubber could improve some high-temperature and rutting-resistance properties of pavements. In Michigan, the goal was less to replace conventional asphalt immediately than to find a useful outlet for a troublesome material. An old tyre that might otherwise have become waste could instead become part of the road that carries schoolchildren each day.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US House bill proposes raising serious H-1B violation fines from $35,000 to $250,000 and extending employer bans from at least 3 years to 10 years as Washington’s visa crackdown intensifies
articles.summary: A new bill in the US House proposes raising H-1B visa violation fines from $35,000 to $250,000 and extending employer bans from 3 years to 10 years, amid intensified scrutiny of the foreign-worker system under the Trump administration.
articles.body: A Republican lawmaker in the US House has introduced legislation that would significantly increase the penalties facing employers found to have committed serious violations of the H-1B visa programme, as scrutiny of the foreign-worker system grows under the Trump administration.The H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, introduced by Texas Republican Rep. Beth Van Duyne on October 1, proposes raising the maximum fine for serious violations from $35,000 to $250,000. It would also extend the period during which companies could be barred from participating in immigration programmes.The bill is part of a wider effort in Congress and the Trump administration to tighten oversight of the H-1B system, which allows US employers to hire foreign workers for specialised occupations.Proposed penalties would rise sharplyUnder Van Duyne's proposal, the minimum ban on employers found responsible for serious H-1B violations would increase from three years to 10 years. The legislation would also raise the fine for another category of violations from $5,000 to $100,000, while extending the minimum exclusion period from two years to five years.The bill also targets fraudulent documentation. Penalties currently ranging from $250 to $2,000 would increase to between $1,000 and $10,000. Another existing fine range of $2,000 to $5,000 would rise to between $20,000 and $50,000.Van Duyne has argued that stronger financial penalties are necessary to deter employers from deliberately breaking H-1B rules and to protect American workers. She has previously sought investigations into suspected H-1B fraud in North Texas.Bill still needs approval from CongressVan Duyne's legislation is not yet law. It has been introduced in the House and sent to the House Judiciary Committee for consideration.Five other Texas Republicans, Brandon Gill, Pete Sessions, Keith Self, Brian Babin and Pat Fallon, are listed as cosponsors.For the proposed penalties to take effect, the legislation would have to pass both the House and Senate and then receive the president's signature.H-1B programme faces wider changesThe proposal follows a broader push by the Trump administration to tighten rules around the H-1B program.In 2025, the administration introduced a $100,000 payment for certain H-1B workers entering the US. A federal judge struck down the measure in June, and the administration has appealed the decision.The Department of Homeland Security has also proposed a $103,265 fee for certain cap-subject H-1B petitions in addition to existing filing costs.Other proposed changes concern how applicants are selected for H-1B visas. articles.title: In 2021, 94-year-old Texas teacher Opal Lee saw Juneteenth become a federal holiday after more than 40 years of activism and a 1,400-mile walk campaign
articles.summary: Discover how 94-year-old Opal Lee's decades of activism and a 1,400-mile walk campaign led to Juneteenth becoming a federal holiday in 2021. Explore her inspiring journey and impact on history.
articles.body: 94-year-old retired Texas teacher Opal Lee stood beside President Joe Biden on June 17, 2021, as he signed the legislation that made Juneteenth a federal holiday. Lee had begun a campaign that took her more than 1,400 miles from Fort Worth to Washington, D.C. five years earlier, when she pushed lawmakers to recognize June 19 nationally.Lee's campaign was a result of decades of work around Juneteenth, which is the holiday that commemorates June 19, 1865, when Union Major Gen. Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston and announced that enslaved people in Texas were free. The Emancipation Proclamation had been issued more than two years earlier, but the news and enforcement of emancipation had not reached many enslaved Texans. The National Archives identifies General Order No. 3, issued by Granger on June 19, 1865, as the document that was associated with Juneteenth's origin.She started walking at 89Lee began her national holiday campaign in 2016 at the age of 89, with her plan being to walk from Fort Worth to Washington, D.C., and cover about 1,400 miles to bring the issue directly to communities and lawmakers along the route. Lee and her supporters traveled to cities that hosted Juneteenth events, and she walked 2.5 miles in each location. The distance was a representation of the roughly two and a half years between President Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation in 1863 and Granger's announcement in Texas in 1865. PBS reported that Lee's campaign eventually drew people from across the country into the effort. Lee worked with organizations with the aim of recognising Juneteenth, organized events and supported petitions that called for federal recognition. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture describes her as integral in the movement that resulted in Juneteenth becoming a federal holiday.Lee grew up in Marshall, Texas, and later moved to Fort Worth. When she was 12, in 1939, her family's Fort Worth home was burned by a white mob on Juneteenth. The house had been purchased by her father and was in a neighborhood where Black families had faced continuous hostility. The Smithsonian says the incident became part of the history behind Lee's later advocacy.Biden signed the bill in 2021The federal campaign gained momentum over the years, especially as Juneteenth received greater national attention during the racial justice demonstrations of 2020. Congress passed legislation that established Juneteenth National Independence Day as a federal holiday in June 2021. Biden signed the bill on June 17, which made Juneteenth the first new federal holiday since Martin Luther King Jr. Day was established in 1983. Lee attended the White House signing ceremony, and the National Archives records June 17, 2021, as the date the legislation was signed into law. Lee continued her annual 2.5-mile Juneteenth walks after the federal designation, which retained the same distance that had become connected with her campaign, while her advocacy became something bigger than the holiday itself.Lee described Juneteenth in broader terms when she spoke to PBS in 2023, and said that it was not limited to Texas or Black Americans but concerned freedom on a wider spectrum. The federal holiday had become part of the national calendar by then, while Lee remained involved in public events and discussions about its history. Her 1,400-mile campaign did not create the federal holiday by itself, and the legislation required congressional action and years of organizing by many people and groups. But Lee's public campaign gave the push a highly visible face, and she was present when the law finally took effect.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: FDR’s grandson bought 150 acres of Texas ranch land in 1999; 27 years later, he has assembled a 1,300-acre family retreat with seven miles of trails
articles.summary: A ranch in Cooke County, north of Dallas, can look as though it has always been there.
articles.body: A ranch in Cooke County, north of Dallas, can look as though it has always been there. Rolling grassland gives way to hardwoods, pecan groves and limestone country, with Clear Creek running through the property. Yet the 1,300-acre Rolling R Ranch was assembled over time rather than acquired as one large holding. Elliot “Tony” Roosevelt Jr., a grandson of Franklin D. Roosevelt, bought the first 150 acres in 1999 and gradually added neighbouring parcels. More than two decades later, the family retreat has become a substantial working ranch with a house, guest accommodation, horse facilities, cattle country and more than seven miles of trails. As reported by the Wall Street Journal, it is now being offered for $21.5 million.Roosevelt turned a 150-acre purchase into a vast North Texas ranchRoosevelt, a Dallas oil and gas executive, did not start out with the full expanse now known as Rolling R Ranch. Reportedly, the initial purchase in 1999 covered 150 acres. From there, adjoining pieces were acquired over the years, eventually bringing the property together as a contiguous ranch of about 1,300 acres. The gradual approach changed the character of the place. Rather than being planned as a large estate from the outset, the ranch developed parcel by parcel. The ranch sits in the Clear Creek Valley, roughly 75 minutes from the Dallas-Fort Worth area and about 30 miles south of the Oklahoma border.The Texas ranch combines working land with wildlife habitatRoosevelt appears to have treated the surrounding land as part of the ranch experience rather than simply as space around a house. The property now includes native grasslands, mature hardwoods and pecan groves, with cattle operations continuing alongside wildlife habitat and outdoor recreation.There are also significant changes in elevation. A limestone ridge runs for more than three miles, while a waterfall sits among the rock formations. Eleven stock ponds are spread across the ranch, and the landscape provides habitat for wildlife including white-tailed deer and Rio Grande turkey.More than seven miles of trails were developed across the property. They pass through wooded ridges, creek corridors and open pasture, creating routes for walking, riding and other outdoor use. The trails are one of the clearest signs of how the ranch was shaped over time: not just as a place to stay, but as a landscape intended to be travelled through.Roosevelt built the ranch around family life and open landFor the Roosevelt family, Rolling R became a weekend property and a place for family gatherings. Reports on the ranch describe children and grandchildren spending time there riding horses, fishing, camping and exploring the creek and surrounding countryside.Its relative proximity to Dallas made that practical. The ranch is around an hour or a little more from the metropolitan area, depending on the starting point, while DFW International Airport is about 65 miles away. Despite that access, the property occupies a distinctly rural setting.The family did not rush into building the main lodge. According to material released by the listing company, Roosevelt waited until neighbouring land could be secured before constructing the hilltop lodge, allowing the surrounding views to remain protected. The same approach was used in the development of trails and outdoor areas.Wildlife measures were incorporated too, including owl boxes, bluebird houses and protected sanctuary areas around the residences. The ranch has also continued to support grazing and native grassland management.Rolling R Ranch combines a modern home with working facilitiesAs reported, the principal residence is a 3,716-square-foot house completed in 2014. It has four bedrooms and four-and-a-half bathrooms, along with an open living area, stone fireplace, granite-topped kitchen and screened porch. Outside, there is a swimming pool and hot tub.The house is only part of the built infrastructure. A 2,800-square-foot barndominium dates from 2001 and functions as ranch headquarters as well as extra accommodation. Its upper level contains bedrooms, while the lower section incorporates working space connected to the property's equestrian facilities.Beside it is a four-stall horse barn with a dedicated tack room. The arrangement gives the property a practical ranch component rather than making it simply a large country residence.The 1,300-acre ranch is now on the marketAs reported by Chron, Rolling R Ranch was listed in 2026 for $21.5 million. At 1,300 acres, that works out to roughly $16,500 per acre. The listing is being handled by Hortenstine Ranch Company.The sale brings an end to a period of nearly three decades in which the property grew from its original 150 acres into a much larger holding. articles.title: Federal executive with top-secret clearance created a fake classified program and diverted $145 million into luxury property and gold; after FBI found 298 gold bars, he pleaded guilty to a $193.6 million fraud
articles.summary: A former senior federal employee with a top-secret security clearance has pleaded guilty to defrauding the US government of approximately $193.6 million,
articles.body: A former senior federal employee with a top-secret security clearance has pleaded guilty to defrauding the US government of approximately $193.6 million, allegedly using fabricated government authorities to obtain money for himself. According to the US Department of Justice, David J. Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, created fictitious government mechanisms, including a fake Special Access Program, to obtain federal funds. Prosecutors said he then acquired gold bars and directed about $145 million in wire transfers towards luxury real estate, watches and at least one car. An FBI search of his home later uncovered 298 gold bars, along with more than $2.1 million in cash and other valuables.How the alleged scheme workedRush held a senior executive-level position at a federal agency and had a Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) security clearance, according to court documents cited by the DOJ. Prosecutors allege that Rush abused that position to create fictitious government authorities that appeared to have legitimate purposes.One of those was a fabricated Special Access Program, a type of highly restricted government programme. According to the DOJ, Rush used these false authorities to obtain US government funds that he intended to use for his own benefit. The government says Rush had also lied about aspects of his education and military experience in reaching his senior position. Ultimately, prosecutors say the scheme resulted in Rush fraudulently obtaining approximately $193,590,400 in federal funds.Millions moved into luxury purchasesOnce the money was obtained, Rush allegedly began moving large amounts of it into assets that had little connection to legitimate government activity. According to the DOJ, he acquired gold bars and directed approximately $145 million in wire transfers that were ultimately used to purchase luxury real estate, watches and at least one vehicle.The gold purchases alone represented tens of millions of dollars. Prosecutors said Rush obtained 298 gold bars at an approximate cost of $46 million to the government. The case therefore involved not just the alleged theft of federal funds but also the misuse of the security protocols and authority associated with a senior government position.FBI search uncovered gold and cashThe scale of the alleged operation became clearer after the FBI searched Rush's residence on May 19, 2026. Agents found 298 gold bars, approximately $2,106,550 in cash, €104,795 and numerous luxury watches, according to the DOJ. The government is now seeking to recover the assets connected to the scheme. Under his plea agreement, Rush agreed to forfeit the gold bars and currency found at his home, along with the properties allegedly purchased with fraud proceeds. He also agreed to forfeit 30 watches, many of them Rolexes, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles. At least one of the BMWs is valued at approximately $172,000, according to prosecutors.Internal investigation led to FBI referralThe case began with an internal investigation that identified potential criminal activity. The CIA said it referred the matter to the FBI after its investigation raised concerns about Rush's conduct. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said Rush had abused his position and betrayed the public trust. The FBI then investigated the alleged misuse of government resources and the movement of the money into personal assets.The case also has a national-security dimension because of Rush's access to sensitive government information. The FBI said his actions involved the manipulation of security protocols intended to protect highly sensitive information. The DOJ said the Director of National Intelligence has requested that the Inspector General for the Intelligence Community conduct a separate investigation.Rush faces up to 20 years in prisonRush pleaded guilty on October 6, 2026, to executing the scheme to defraud the federal government. He is scheduled to be sentenced on January 28, 2027. He faces a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, along with up to three years of supervised release, forfeiture, restitution and a fine. The final sentence will be decided by a federal judge after consideration of the US Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The Justice Department's investigation remains ongoing.The case stands out not only because of the nearly $194 million involved, but also because of how the money was allegedly obtained. Prosecutors say Rush used the authority and credibility attached to a senior federal position and a TS/SCI clearance to create a fictional government structure, obtain public funds and then convert much of that money into personal wealth.
